study.title: Joshua 10 - The Lord fights for Israel in the Southern Campaign
study.overview: The chapter describes Joshua's immediate response to the attack on Gibeon, the defeat of the coalition of five Amorites kings and the successive takeover of several southern Canaan cities. The central point is not only Israel's military strategy, but the decisive action of the Lord: He encourages Joshua, confuses the enemy, shed stones from heaven and prolongs the day to complete victory. The chapter ends with Joshua returning to Gilgal after a successful campaign, which prepares for the continuation of the conquest.

outline.title: The coalition of the kings against Gibeon
outline.explanation: Knowing that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, the king of Jerusalem gathers four Amorite kings together. Fear of Israeli expansion leads these rulers to attack Gibeon together, treating Israel's new alliance as a strategic threat.

outline.title: The help of Gibeon and the intervention of God
outline.explanation: The Gibeonites ask for help from Joshua, who goes up from Gilgal with his men. The Lord encourages you not to fear, because victory is already decided. The battle intensifies with great death, stones from heaven and the episode in which the sun and moon are sent to detain, showing that the Lord fights for Israel.

outline.title: The Five Kings Rejoicing and Runed
outline.explanation: The kings hide in a pit, but are found, exposed and placed under public defeat. Joshua makes the war leaders put their feet on their necks, reinforcing the assurance that the Lord will do the same to the rest of the enemies. Then the kings are killed and hung until the end of the day, and the pit is sealed.

outline.title: Expansion of conquest and return to Gilgal
outline.explanation: Joshua takes Makkedah, Libnah, and Lachish, Eglon, and Hebron, defeating kings and cities of the mountainous region, of the southern, of the plains, and of the coasts. The text insists that this occurred because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel. The section concludes with Joshua and all the people returning to the camp in Gilgal.

study.context: The given notes place this chapter as part of the second major section of the book, dedicated to Joshua's campaigns in the south and then in the north of Canaan. Gibeon and surrounding towns were on a platform north of Jerusalem; with Gibeon beside Israel, control of this region favored the domination of the country's interior. No more secure historical context is given more than that.
study.theology: The chapter presents a clear theology of holy warfare under the Lord's initiative. Joshua acts quickly, but victory is not attributed to human talent; the Lord Himself delivers enemies, troubles his armies, sends stones from heaven, and answers to Joshua's prayer. The prolongation of the day expresses that creation is under the authority of God and that powers considered strong, including the sun and the moon, cannot resist its purpose. The humiliation of kings also reinforces that the triumph of Israel is a sign of God's faithfulness to his word and judgment upon the enemies that oppose his people.

scholarViews.insight: Gibeon's alliance with Israel changed the balance of regional control, as the possession of this platform favored the domination of the interior of Canaan.
The obedience of Joshua to help the Gibeonites shows readiness and righteousness, and victory is presented as advancement led by the Lord, not as a mere human being made.
The chapter insists that the defeat of the kings and the taking of their lands took place in a single campaign, because the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel.

questions: What does the chapter teach about acting with courage when God has already promised presence and victory?
How does the Lord's direct intervention correct the tendency to attribute results only to human capacity?
How does the humiliation of the five kings help to understand the seriousness of God's judgment on opposition to their purpose?
study.practice: Trust God's initiative and respond with immediate obedience, as Joshua did when he left Gilgal. When there is external pressure, pray and act without paralysis, remembering that the battle belongs to the Lord. Also learn to recognize that real victories do not serve for self-exaltation, but to strengthen faith in the God who fights for his people and fulfills his word.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text here is long and includes a quotation from an ancient book mentioned in Joshua 10:13, but the notes do not explain its nature or provide external confirmation; therefore, one should not say more than the chapter presents. There is also no base notes to safely identify additional historical details about cities beyond what was explicitly said.
